paragraphs.text: Lesson 24, invitations and offers.
Conversation number one, informal invitations.
Anna wants to hang out with her friends this weekend.
Listen to her phone calls.
Hi Betty, are you doing anything tomorrow afternoon?
No, I don't have any plans.
Do you want to see a movie?
There's a mat-nay of the new James Bond film at 245.
Sure.
Why don't you give Nate a call and ask him if he wants to go too?
Hey Nate, what are you up to tomorrow?
Not much, why?
How about seeing a movie with me and Betty?
Yeah, alright. What time?
We're going to meet up at the theater at 230.
Oh wait, actually, I don't think I can go.
I have to pick up my brother from soccer practice. It ends at 330.
I'll have to take a rain check.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
Anna uses two phrases to ask about Betty's and Nate's availability.
Here are some additional options.
Are you doing anything tomorrow afternoon?
What are you up to tomorrow?
Do you have any plans for this weekend?
What you doing on Friday?
Then she uses some of these phrases to invite Betty and Nate.
Do you want to see a movie?
How about seeing a movie?
Care to see a movie?
How would you like to see a movie?
Why don't we see a movie?
Let's see a movie.
If you also want to offer to pay for the other person, you can add one of these phrases.
How about having a drink after work?
I'm buying.
Let's grab some lunch, my treat.
Care to get some ice cream? It's on me.
To say yes to an informal invitation, you can say...
Sure. Sounds good.
Yeah, alright.
Count me in.
We usually say count me in only if it is a group of people going.
To say no to an informal invitation, you can say...
I don't think I can.
I'd love to, but...
I can't. I gotta pick up my brother from school.
Or I can't. I have to pick up my brother from school.
I'll have to take a rain check.
This means you can't go, but you hope the person invites you again in the future.
Conversation number two, formal invitations.
Now listen to Anna's conversations as she talks with her co-workers.
Hi, Cindy. Are you free today at lunchtime?
Yes, I think so.
A few of us from the marketing department are going to an Italian restaurant in the neighborhood.
Would you like to join us?
I'd love to, thanks.
Hi, Paul. I know it's short notice, but my husband and I were wondering if you'd like to go to a baseball game on Saturday. We have an extra ticket.
I'd love to, but I'm afraid to have another commitment this weekend.
Oh, well. Maybe another time.
Yeah. Why don't you ask Chris? He's into baseball.
Chris, my husband and I have an extra ticket for Saturday's baseball game. Would you like to come?
I wish I could, but I'll actually be away on a business trip.
Ah, that's too bad. Do you know anyone else who might be interested?
How about Rachel?
Rachel, would you like to go to a baseball game on Saturday?
That's very kind of you, but I have other plans. Sorry.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
From these conversations, we learn more formal phrases for inviting people.
Are you free or are you available? I know it's short notice, but use this phrase when you are inviting people.
I'd love to say something very soon.
Would you like to?
I was wondering if you'd like to. To say yes to a more formal invitation, you can say.
That would be nice. I'd love to. I'd be delighted to join you.
To say no to a more formal invitation, you can say. I'd love to, but I'm afraid I have another commitment.
I wish I could, but unfortunately.
That's very kind of you, but I have other plans.
We also see Anna's reactions to her colleagues' refusals, she says.
Oh well, maybe another time. That's too bad. That's a shame.
Now, what do you say if someone invites you, but you can't give a yes or no answer immediately?
Here are some phrases for that situation.
Let me check my calendar.
I'm not sure what my plans are. Could I get back to you tomorrow?
I might be able to go, but I'm not sure. Could I let you know a little later?
Conversation number three, making and responding to offers.
Erica is a college student, and she has invited her boyfriend's mother to her apartment for lunch.
She wants to be a good hostess, so she does everything possible to make polite offers.
Hi Mrs. Kennedy, come on in.
Please, call me Margaret.
Alright, can I take your coat? Thanks.
Please, make yourself at home. May I offer you something to drink?
Acapity would be great.
Okay, would you like milk or sugar?
Just some sugar, please.
How about some cookies, too?
Oh, no, thank you. I'm on a diet.
Okay, I made a chicken salad for lunch. Can I get you some?
That's very kind of you, Eric, but I'm actually a vegetarian.
Ah, I didn't know that, but I'll prepare a salad without chicken if you like.
That would be great. Would you like some help in the kitchen?
No, that's alright.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases. Here are some phrases from making offers.
May I offer you some tea? Can I get you something to drink?
Would you like some mashed potatoes?
Would you like an apple? Do you want some dessert?
Do you want a ride home? How about some chips? How about a beer?
I'll wash the dishes if you like. I'll lend you an umbrella if you want.
In these phrases, may I offer you is the most formal.
Do you want and how about are informal?
The most common phrase which you can use in both formal and informal situations is,
would you like? Here are some ways to say yes to an offer.
May I offer you some tea? Thank you. I'd love a cup of tea.
Can I get you anything to drink? Some coffee would be great, thanks.
Would you like a piece of cake? Or do you want a piece of cake?
Yes, please. I'll wash the dishes if you like.
Thanks, that's a very kind of you. Or thanks, I appreciate it.
Here are some ways to say no to an offer politely. May I offer you a cigar? Thanks, but I don't smoke.
Can I get you something to eat? That's very kind of you, but I've just had lunch.
Would you like a beer? Or how about some pizza? No, thank you.
Or no thanks. I'll turn up the air conditioning if you like. No, that's okay.
You've finished lesson 24. Now take the quiz to practice the variations on the invitation and offer phrases.
